summary: D284 is a software engineering course with no coding: you learn process models, requirements engineering, design concepts and software quality, then show them in one performance assessment: by student accounts, a written proposal in which you act as project lead recommending a CRM system for a mid-sized company, either a configurable off-the-shelf product or a custom build. The proposal draws on the whole course, from scope and requirements to a development methodology, design visuals and test cases. A 2024 first-try passer wrote it in about two days, while a 2025 student was returned three times over visuals that didn't match the CRM.
author: Dorian Acosta

assessment.type: Performance assessment: a written CRM system proposal (reported), evaluator-graded
assessment.format: 1 written task (reported) · a CRM proposal built on WGU's requirements document and design template (one 2024 passer's ran 14 pages) · rubric-graded, no exam
details: The task (reported): in general terms (your task page has the exact requirements), you act as the project lead proposing a customer relationship management (CRM) system for a medium-sized company, and you choose between a customizable commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) product and a custom build. WGU provides a CRM requirements document and a design template to work from. The proposal describes the project and its environment, states its requirements, compares development methodologies and picks one, illustrates features with visuals, and gives test cases.

Length and grading: a 2024 passer's paper ran 14 pages and took about two days, and 2025 commenters say a few hours is possible once the structure is clear. Evaluators grade against the rubric and return the paper with feedback when an item falls short (WGU's general PA process); one 2025 student was returned three times over visuals that didn't match the CRM.
Course facts: BSCS 202412 (Jan 2026 catalog) lists D284 (4 CU) in term 7. B.S. Software Engineering (202610) and B.S. AI Engineering (202607) also list it.
tips: Build your outline from the rubric's letters and use them as headings, so the evaluator finds each item exactly where they expect it.

Keep the CRM requirements document and the design template open while you write. Reuse their names and wording, and label every requirement (BR1, UR1, FR1, NFR1) so your visuals and test cases can point back to it.
Make the visuals match the text: the same feature names, fields and steps as your requirements, and a short explanation under each.
Watch the instructor webinar recordings and read the common fail points document in the course resources before drafting; they show what evaluators check most often.
Write test cases someone else could run without asking you anything: preconditions, numbered steps, specific data and an observable expected result.
Justify instead of just describing. Tie each reason for your methodology to facts in the scenario, and compare COTS and custom on cost, time, fit and risk.
Fix Grammarly's correctness suggestions before you submit, and cite any source you quote or paraphrase.
If evaluator feedback contradicts the written requirements or guidance your instructor gave you, students describe appealing, with the instructor's emails as evidence.

competencies: Course planning: discuss your course planning tool report with your instructor and create your personalized course plan together (listed first in the program guidebook).
The learner analyzes the objectives, scope, and organizational impact of software systems.
The learner creates test cases for quality assurance as part of software development processes.
The learner determines optimal software design for given requirements.
The learner identifies the costs and impact of design changes to software systems.

topics.title: Software engineering and the generic process framework
topics.eli5: Software engineering is building software the way engineers build bridges: with a plan, a process and checks at every stage instead of just starting to code.
topics.detail: D284 covers no programming; it's about the discipline around the code. The catalog says a generic process framework provides the groundwork for formal process models. In Pressman's widely used textbook, that framework is five activities: communication (understand stakeholders and gather requirements), planning (estimates, schedule, risks and resources), modeling (analysis and design models that clarify requirements and the design), construction (code generation and testing) and deployment (delivery, support and feedback). Umbrella activities run across all five: project tracking and control, risk management, quality assurance, technical reviews, measurement, configuration management, reusability management and work-product preparation. Each process model arranges the same activities differently: waterfall runs them once in sequence, while incremental, iterative and agile models repeat them in short cycles. OpenStax's free textbook frames the same idea as four phases (inception, elaboration, construction and deployment), so terminology varies between sources; use your course material's terms in your paper.
points: Framework activities: communication · planning · modeling · construction · deployment
Umbrella activities apply throughout: risk management, quality assurance, technical reviews, configuration management and measurement
"Disciplined" means repeatable: defined steps, reviewed work products and controlled changes
The PA casts you as the project lead, so think in these activities: whom you talk to, what you plan, what you model, how you test and how you deliver

topics.title: Prescriptive process models: waterfall to the Unified Process
topics.eli5: Process models are recipes for running a project: some say do every step once in order, and others say cook a little, taste it and adjust.
topics.detail: Prescriptive models define an ordered set of activities and work products. Waterfall runs requirements, design, implementation, testing and deployment in sequence, and each phase ends with documents and a sign-off before the next starts. It suits stable, well-understood requirements and heavy documentation needs, but changes are costly and working software arrives late. The V-model pairs each development stage with a test level: requirements with acceptance testing, system design with system testing, architecture with integration testing and module design with unit testing. The incremental model delivers the system in usable pieces, core features first, so users get value early. Prototyping builds quick mock-ups to pin down unclear requirements, and rapid application development (RAD) compresses the schedule with prototypes, reusable components and heavy user involvement. Boehm's spiral model repeats cycles of setting objectives, analyzing and reducing risks, developing and testing, and planning the next round, which fits large or high-risk projects. The Unified Process runs iterations through four phases: inception, elaboration, construction and transition (Pressman's textbook adds a fifth, production, covering ongoing use and support).
points: Waterfall: predictable and documentation-heavy, weak at absorbing change
V-model: plan each test level while you write the matching specification
Incremental: each increment is a working subset, such as contacts first, then the sales pipeline, then reporting
Spiral: risk drives each loop; choose it when a wrong guess would be expensive
Unified Process phases: inception → elaboration → construction → transition

topics.title: Agile, Scrum and Kanban
topics.eli5: Agile teams build software in small slices, show each slice to the customer and steer by what they learn, like driving with your eyes on the road instead of only on the map.
topics.detail: The 2001 Agile Manifesto values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan, while still valuing the items on the right. Its twelve principles include delivering working software frequently, welcoming changing requirements and having business people and developers work together daily. The 2020 Scrum Guide defines three accountabilities: a Product Owner who maximizes value and orders the Product Backlog, a Scrum Master who makes the team effective by coaching and removing impediments, and Developers who build each Increment. It also defines five events (the Sprint, one month or less, containing Sprint Planning, a 15-minute Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective) and three artifacts, each with a commitment: the Product Backlog with the Product Goal, the Sprint Backlog with the Sprint Goal, and the Increment with the Definition of Done. Kanban visualizes work on a board, limits work in progress (WIP) and manages flow, with no fixed iterations or prescribed roles. Extreme Programming (XP) adds engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development and continuous integration.
points: Scrum timeboxes for a one-month Sprint: Planning up to 8 hours, Review up to 4, Retrospective up to 3, Daily Scrum 15 minutes
User story format: As a <role>, I want <capability>, so that <benefit>
Agile still plans and documents; it plans over shorter horizons and keeps the documentation that's useful
Kanban fits steady streams of small work, such as configuration requests after a CRM goes live
Extreme Programming (XP) adds engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development and continuous integration

topics.title: Comparing and choosing an SDLC methodology
topics.eli5: Choosing a methodology is like choosing a vehicle: a train is great when the track is fixed, and a car is better when you expect detours.
topics.detail: A methodology choice is only as strong as its comparison: weigh the candidates side by side, then choose one and justify it for this CRM project. A strong comparison applies the same criteria to each, ideally in a small table: how each handles changing requirements, when working software first reaches users, how much up-front planning and documentation it needs, how it manages risk, how involved the customer must be, what team size and experience it assumes, and how it fits the delivery approach (configuring a COTS product or building a custom one). The justification then ties the choice to facts in the scenario instead of general praise. Unclear or evolving user needs and a business that wants early value favor iterative or agile delivery, while fixed requirements, a fixed-price contract or regulatory sign-offs favor waterfall or the V-model. Hybrids are common, such as a short up-front requirements and architecture phase followed by sprints, and naming a weakness of your choice along with how you'll manage it shows judgment.
points: Criteria to compare: requirement stability · risk · time to first release · documentation · customer involvement · team skills · cost predictability
COTS rollouts are often configured in iterations so stakeholders can review each configured module
State the choice in one sentence first, then give two or three reasons drawn from the scenario
Name one weakness and its mitigation, such as scope creep in agile handled by a prioritized backlog

topics.title: CRM systems and the build-or-buy decision
topics.eli5: A CRM is a company's shared memory of every customer: who they are, what they bought, what they asked for and what should happen next.
topics.detail: Customer relationship management (CRM) software centralizes customer and prospect records and the history of every interaction. Typical modules are contact and account management, the sales pipeline (leads, opportunities and forecasts), marketing automation, customer service cases or tickets, reporting and dashboards, and integrations with email, calendars, accounting and other systems. The reported task makes you choose between a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) product, which NIST defines as ready-made hardware or software available for purchase by the public, configured and extended for the company, and a custom system built to fit. COTS usually wins on time to launch, up-front cost, vendor-maintained security and upgrades, and proven features, but it brings ongoing subscription costs, limits on customization, dependence on the vendor's roadmap and possible lock-in. A custom build fits unusual processes exactly and keeps ownership in-house, but it costs more, takes longer and leaves maintenance, security and hosting to the company. Compare total cost of ownership over several years, not just the first invoice: licenses or development, implementation, customization, integration, data migration, training, support and upgrades.
points: Configuration (settings and fields the product supports) is cheaper and safer than customization (custom code), which can complicate upgrades
Most COTS CRMs are sold as software as a service, so the vendor hosts and updates them
A gap analysis drives the decision: which requirements the product meets out of the box, which need configuration and which need custom work
Data migration from spreadsheets or an old system is a project of its own: cleanup, field mapping, trial loads and a cutover plan
Three CRM types are often named: operational (sales, service and marketing processes), analytical (insight from customer data) and collaborative (customer data shared across teams)

topics.title: Purpose, problems, goals, objectives and scope
topics.eli5: Before you build anything, you write down why you're building it, what's broken today, how you'll know it worked and where the project stops.
topics.detail: The proposal's opening sections answer the first competency: the objectives, scope and organizational impact of the system. The purpose says why the project exists in business terms. Problem statements describe today's pain points, such as scattered spreadsheets, duplicate records, missed follow-ups or no view of the sales pipeline, and each one is paired with how the proposed system addresses it. Goals are broad outcomes, such as better customer retention, while objectives are specific, measurable steps toward a goal, best written in SMART form: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Scope lists what the project will deliver (in scope) and what it explicitly won't (out of scope); a clear out-of-scope list prevents scope creep and sets expectations. Prerequisites are conditions that must be in place before or during the project, such as hardware, network capacity, licenses, accounts, data cleanup or staff availability, and giving each one a date turns the list into a plan. Assumptions (believed true but unverified) and constraints (fixed limits such as budget, deadline or regulations) complete the picture.
points: Goal: improve customer retention · objective: raise the repeat-purchase rate from 30% to 40% within 12 months of launch
Pair each problem with its fix: the problem → who it hurts → how the CRM solves it
Out of scope lists real nearby work you won't do (a new website, payroll, a mobile app), not filler
A prerequisites table can carry the item, its type, an owner and a target date

topics.title: Environment, hosting and architecture
topics.eli5: The environment is the system's address and toolbox: where it lives, which devices and browsers people use to reach it, and what it's built with.
topics.detail: An environment section describes everything around the system. On the client side, list the operating systems and browsers staff will use, typically current Windows and macOS versions with current Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari, plus any mobile access. Hosting follows NIST's cloud definitions. In software as a service (SaaS), the provider runs the application and everything beneath it; in platform as a service (PaaS), the provider runs the platform and you deploy your own code; and in infrastructure as a service (IaaS), you rent servers, storage and networks and manage the operating system and everything above it. On-premises hosting puts the servers in the company's own facility, and NIST's cloud deployment models are public, private, community and hybrid. A custom CRM is usually described as a three-tier architecture: a front end or presentation tier (HTML, CSS and a JavaScript framework), a back end or application tier (for example Java with Spring, C# with .NET, or Node.js) and a data tier (a relational database such as PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server), connected through APIs. Name the languages, the IDEs (IntelliJ IDEA, Visual Studio or VS Code, for example) and version control such as Git. A COTS CRM still has an environment: the vendor's hosting, the browsers it supports, its configuration tools and any extension language it offers.
points: Reported tip: take the hosting details from the requirements document

SaaS: the vendor runs the application and everything beneath it, and you manage your users, data and settings · PaaS: you manage your code and data · IaaS: you manage the OS and up · on-premises: you manage it all
Name versions where they matter, such as a supported-browser list, and justify each choice in a sentence
Separate development, test and production environments so changes are tried before they reach users

topics.title: Requirements engineering: types and how to write them
topics.eli5: Requirements are the promises a system makes, written so plainly that anyone can check whether each promise was kept.
topics.detail: The IIBA's BABOK Guide (version 3) sorts requirements into four groups. Business requirements state the goals and outcomes that explain why the change is happening. Stakeholder requirements state what particular people or groups need, bridging business and solution requirements; many courses call these user requirements. Solution requirements describe the system: functional requirements say what it must do (its behavior and the information it manages), and non-functional requirements say how well it must do it or under what conditions. Transition requirements are temporary needs for moving from the current state to the future state, such as data conversion and training. Requirements engineering runs through elicitation (interviews, workshops, observation, surveys and document analysis), analysis, specification, validation (are these the right requirements?) and change management. Good requirements are necessary, unambiguous, singular (one need each), feasible, verifiable and traceable, and are conventionally written as "The system shall …". Labeling each one (BR1, UR1, FR1, NFR1) lets later sections, visuals and test cases point back to it.
points: Business: increase repeat sales · user: reps need one view of each customer's history · functional: the system shall log calls and emails against a contact · non-functional: the history page shall load within 2 seconds
Verifiable means a test can pass or fail it; "user-friendly" can't be tested until you define how it's measured
Reported tip: label each requirement and mirror the requirements document's wording in its subsection
A traceability matrix maps each requirement to the design elements and test cases that cover it

topics.title: Non-functional requirements and quality attributes
topics.eli5: Functional requirements say what the system does, and non-functional requirements say how fast, how safe and how dependable it is while doing it.
topics.detail: ISO/IEC 25010, the product quality model, is a ready-made checklist for non-functional requirements. Its current edition names nine characteristics: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability (formerly usability), reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility (formerly portability) and safety. Each non-functional requirement should name a measurable target and the conditions it applies under. Examples: response time (95% of searches return within 2 seconds with 200 concurrent users), availability (99.9% monthly uptime, excluding scheduled maintenance), security (role-based access, all traffic encrypted with TLS, no passwords stored in plain text), recoverability (restore from backup within 4 hours, losing no more than 1 hour of data), compatibility (works in the current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari), accessibility (meets WCAG 2.2 level AA) and scalability (handles 50% user growth without redesign). Compliance needs, such as privacy laws that govern customer data, often become non-functional requirements too.
points: Reliability's subcharacteristics in the current model: faultlessness, availability, fault tolerance and recoverability
Security's subcharacteristics: confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, authenticity and resistance
99.9% availability allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month; 99.99% allows about 4
State the target and how you'd measure it; a non-functional requirement with no number can't be tested

topics.title: Design concepts and visual models
topics.eli5: Design is deciding how the pieces fit before you build them, and diagrams are the blueprints that let other people check your thinking.
topics.detail: Core design concepts include abstraction (hide detail behind a simpler idea), modularity (split the system into parts), information hiding and encapsulation (each module keeps its internals private), separation of concerns, high cohesion (each module does one job well), low coupling (modules depend on each other as little as possible) and stepwise refinement from high-level to detailed design. Determining the optimal design means choosing the option that best meets the requirements within the constraints, and saying why. Visual models make a design checkable. UML 2.5.1 groups its diagrams into structure diagrams (class, component, deployment and package, among others) and behavior diagrams (use case, activity, state machine, and interaction diagrams such as sequence diagrams). A flowchart shows a process with standard symbols, and a wireframe or mockup shows a screen's layout and controls. Each visual should depict a feature from your requirements, use the same names as the text, and come with a short explanation of what it shows, which requirement it supports and how a user moves through it.
points: Use case diagram: who uses the system for what · activity diagram or flowchart: the steps and decisions in one workflow · sequence diagram: which parts exchange which messages, in order · class diagram: data and relationships
Flowchart symbols: oval for start and end, rectangle for a process step, diamond for a decision, parallelogram for input or output, arrows for flow
Wireframe = low-fidelity layout · mockup = static, realistic visual · prototype = clickable
Reported: explain each visual; a 2025 student's returns came from visuals that didn't match the CRM described
Free tools: diagrams.net (draw.io) for flowcharts and UML, Figma for screen mockups

topics.title: Test cases and software quality
topics.eli5: A test case is a recipe for checking one promise: exactly what to set up, what to do and what should happen, so anyone can repeat it and get the same answer.
topics.detail: Software quality assurance is the planned set of activities that builds confidence a product meets its requirements, and testing is one of them. A test case should be replicable by someone who has never seen the system, with an ID, the requirement it verifies, preconditions (account, role, existing data), numbered steps, specific test data, the expected result, and places for the actual result and a pass or fail. Test levels run from unit testing (one component) through integration testing (components working together) and system testing (the whole system against its requirements) to acceptance testing, where users or the customer confirm it meets their needs (user acceptance testing, or UAT). Black-box techniques choose efficient inputs. Equivalence partitioning tests one representative value from each class of inputs that should behave the same, and boundary value analysis tests values at and just beyond each edge of a valid range. Write positive tests (valid input succeeds) and negative tests (invalid input is rejected with a clear message), and trace every test to a requirement label.
points: Test case fields: ID · requirement · preconditions · steps · test data · expected result · actual result · pass or fail
Valid range 1–100: boundary tests 0, 1, 100 and 101; partition representatives such as −5, 50 and 150
Reported tip: keep tests replicable, give expected results and leave out stress tests
Expected results must be observable, such as "a confirmation appears and the record shows in the list", not "it works"

topics.title: Costs and impact of design changes
topics.eli5: Moving a wall on a blueprint costs an eraser; moving it after the house is built costs a wrecking crew.
topics.detail: One competency asks you to identify the costs and impact of design changes. A late change forces rework in every artifact built on the old decision (requirements, design, code, tests, documentation and training material) plus retesting and redeployment, and once the system is live it can also affect real data and real users. That's why defects and changes caught in requirements and design reviews are far cheaper to fix than the same problems found in production. Impact analysis traces a proposed change through the traceability matrix to everything it touches, then estimates effort, cost, schedule and risk. Change control routes the request to a decision-maker, often a change control board, before work starts, and configuration management keeps versions of every artifact so changes stay controlled and reversible. In a COTS CRM, customizations that stray from the vendor's standard features raise the cost of every future upgrade, and shortcuts in any system create technical debt that's repaid later as extra rework.
points: Impact analysis asks what changes, which requirements, designs, tests and users are affected, and what it costs in time and money
Agile lowers the cost of change with small increments and automated tests, but it doesn't make change free
Configure before you customize; heavy custom code in a COTS product can break on upgrades
Regression testing after each change confirms that what used to work still works

practice.q: Which statement is a non-functional requirement for the CRM?
choices: The system shall let a sales rep log a phone call and its outcome against a customer record.
The system shall open a customer record within 2 seconds for 95% of requests with 200 concurrent users.
The company wants to increase repeat-customer revenue by 10% within a year of the CRM's launch.
Sales managers need to see each rep's open deals, with their expected close dates, in one place.
practice.answer: The system shall open a customer record within 2 seconds for 95% of requests with 200 concurrent users.
practice.why: A non-functional requirement states a quality or constraint, here performance, with a measurable target and the condition it applies under (200 concurrent users). Logging a call is a function the system performs, so it's a functional requirement. Raising repeat revenue explains why the company is investing, which makes it a business requirement, and what sales managers need is a stakeholder (user) requirement that later becomes functional requirements.

practice.q: In the BABOK Guide's classification, which type of requirement explains why the organization is starting the project at all?
choices: Stakeholder requirements
Functional requirements
Business requirements
Transition requirements
practice.why: Business requirements are the goals, objectives and outcomes behind the change: the why. Stakeholder requirements say what particular people or groups need, functional requirements describe what the solution must do, and transition requirements cover temporary needs for the changeover, such as data conversion and training, that disappear once the change is complete.

practice.q: A draft requirement reads: "The CRM should be user-friendly and fast." What's the main problem with it?
choices: It can't be verified, since user-friendly and fast have no measurable target
It's really a functional requirement, so it belongs under a different heading
It uses "should", and a binding requirement has to say "will" instead
It names a specific technology, which requirements are supposed to avoid
practice.answer: It can't be verified, since user-friendly and fast have no measurable target
practice.why: A requirement has to be verifiable: a test must be able to pass or fail it. Rewrite it as separate, measurable statements, such as a response-time target under a stated load and a usability target like the share of new users who complete a task unaided. It also bundles two needs into one, which breaks the singular rule. Swapping "should" for "will" wouldn't fix it: by convention a binding requirement says "shall", and even then the statement would stay untestable. Ease of use and speed are qualities, so this is a non-functional requirement, and it names no technology.

practice.q: Which project is the best fit for a waterfall or V-model approach?
choices: A regulated payroll module with fixed, documented requirements and sign-off at each phase
A new mobile app whose features will be shaped by weekly feedback from its first users
A first-of-its-kind product with high technical risk, where early prototypes must prove the idea
A startup's first release that must reach users in four weeks and will change often after that
practice.answer: A regulated payroll module with fixed, documented requirements and sign-off at each phase
practice.why: Sequential models work best when requirements are stable and well understood and the organization needs documents and approvals at each phase, as regulated work often does; the V-model adds a planned test level for each specification. Feedback-driven features and fast, changing releases call for agile or incremental delivery, and high technical risk with prototypes points to the spiral model or prototyping.

practice.q: What sets Boehm's spiral model apart from other process models?
choices: It completes each phase once, in strict order, with a sign-off before the next one starts
It works in fixed timeboxes of one month or less, pulling its work from a Product Backlog
It manages a continuous flow of work items on a board, with limits on work in progress
It repeats loops that each set objectives and reduce the biggest risks before building
practice.answer: It repeats loops that each set objectives and reduce the biggest risks before building
practice.why: The spiral model is risk-driven: every loop sets objectives, identifies and reduces the biggest risks (often with a prototype), develops and tests, then plans the next loop, which suits large or high-risk projects. Completing each phase once in order with sign-offs describes waterfall, fixed timeboxes fed from a Product Backlog describe Scrum, and limiting work in progress on a continuous flow describes Kanban.

practice.q: In Scrum, who is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog?
choices: The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
The Developers
The project manager
practice.why: The 2020 Scrum Guide makes the Product Owner accountable for maximizing the product's value and for managing the Product Backlog, including ordering it; others can help, but the Product Owner stays accountable. The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness, and the Developers are accountable for the Sprint Backlog, their plan for the Sprint. The whole Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment each Sprint, and Scrum defines no project manager role.

practice.q: Which of these is a SMART objective for the CRM project?
choices: Raise customer satisfaction as high as possible across every sales region
Buy the highest-rated CRM on the market and roll it out to every department
Cut the average ticket resolution time from 48 to 24 hours within six months of launch
Give the sales team better tools within six months of launch so they can close more deals
practice.answer: Cut the average ticket resolution time from 48 to 24 hours within six months of launch
practice.why: It's specific (average support-ticket resolution time), measurable (48 to 24 hours), plausibly achievable, relevant to a CRM's service module and time-bound (six months after launch). Better tools within six months has a deadline but no measurable target, satisfaction "as high as possible" has neither a target nor a deadline, and buying the highest-rated CRM is a choice of solution, not an objective.

practice.q: The CRM project covers contact management, the sales pipeline and support tickets. Which item belongs on the out-of-scope list?
choices: Importing existing customer records into the CRM
Training sales staff on the new pipeline screens
Role-based access so reps see only their own accounts
Replacing the company's payroll system
practice.why: Out of scope lists related work the project explicitly won't do, and payroll is a separate system the CRM doesn't touch. Importing existing records (data migration) and training staff are transition work the rollout needs, and role-based access is a security requirement of the CRM itself, so all three belong in scope.

practice.q: Which is a typical advantage of a COTS CRM over a custom-built one?
choices: Complete control over every feature, over the source code and over the release schedule
Faster deployment and lower up-front cost, since the core features already exist
No subscription or license fees at any point over the system's whole lifetime
A perfect fit for unusual business processes with no configuration work at all
practice.answer: Faster deployment and lower up-front cost, since the core features already exist
practice.why: Commercial off-the-shelf products come with proven features, vendor-managed security and upgrades, and short setup times. In exchange you usually pay ongoing subscription or license fees, accept limits on customization, depend on the vendor's roadmap and still need configuration to fit your processes. Full control over features, source code and release timing is the main argument for a custom build.

practice.q: Under NIST's cloud definitions, a CRM that staff use in a web browser while the vendor runs the servers, the platform and the application itself is which service model?
choices: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
Platform as a service (PaaS)
On-premises hosting
Software as a service (SaaS)
practice.why: In SaaS the provider runs the application and everything beneath it, and the customer uses and configures it, which describes most COTS CRMs. With PaaS you deploy your own application onto the provider's platform, and with IaaS you rent servers, storage and networks and manage the operating system and up. On-premises means the company runs everything in its own facility, and NIST doesn't count it as a cloud service model.

choices: Precondition: user rep01 is logged in with the Sales role. Steps: open the Customers list, pick any customer you like, type a short note of your own and click Save. Expected: the notes feature works correctly for whichever customer you picked.

Precondition: user rep01 is logged in with the Sales role, and customer Acme Corp exists. Steps: open Customers, select Acme Corp, add the note "Follow up Friday" and click Save. Expected: the note appears first in Acme Corp's activity list with today's date.

Precondition: none. Steps: keep adding new users and new customer notes as fast as you can until the system slows down or fails. Expected: the system holds up under the heavy load for as long as it possibly can.

Precondition: several sales reps have used the notes feature for at least a week. Steps: ask each rep whether they like the feature and what they would change. Expected: most of the reps say they are happy with the new notes feature.
practice.answer: Precondition: user rep01 is logged in with the Sales role, and customer Acme Corp exists. Steps: open Customers, select Acme Corp, add the note "Follow up Friday" and click Save. Expected: the note appears first in Acme Corp's activity list with today's date.
practice.why: A replicable test case states the starting state, including the data it needs, then exact steps, specific test data and an observable expected result, so anyone who runs it gets the same pass or fail. Picking any customer and expecting the feature to "work correctly" leaves the data and the outcome up to the tester. Adding users and notes until the system fails is a stress test, which students advise leaving out, and asking reps whether they like a feature is feedback gathering, not a test with a defined outcome.

practice.q: A discount field accepts whole numbers from 0 to 50. Using boundary value analysis, which set of inputs tests the boundaries?
practice.why: Boundary value analysis tests each edge of the valid range and the nearest invalid values just outside it, because off-by-one mistakes cluster there: −1 and 51 should be rejected, while 0 and 50 should be accepted. 0, 25 and 50 skips the invalid neighbors, the values from 10 to 40 sit inside one partition, and −100 and 100 are far from both edges.

practice.q: In Pressman's generic process framework, which activity covers building analysis and design models such as UML diagrams?
choices: Communication
Construction
Deployment
Modeling
practice.why: Modeling creates analysis models that clarify requirements and design models that describe the architecture, components and interfaces, including UML diagrams. Communication gathers requirements from stakeholders, construction covers code generation and testing, and deployment delivers the software and gathers feedback. Planning, the fifth activity, sets the schedule, estimates and risks.

practice.q: Which visual best shows the steps and decision points in converting a sales lead into a customer?
choices: A class diagram
A deployment diagram
An activity diagram or flowchart
An entity-relationship diagram
practice.why: Activity diagrams and flowcharts show a workflow as ordered steps with decisions and branches, such as whether a lead qualifies. Class and entity-relationship diagrams show data structures and relationships, not steps over time, and a deployment diagram shows which software runs on which hardware or nodes.

practice.q: Why does a requirement change usually cost more when it's discovered after the CRM is deployed than during requirements analysis?
choices: Everything built on the old requirement, from design to training, must be reworked and retested
Most process models forbid any change to requirements once the requirements phase has been signed off
COTS vendors charge a fixed fee for every change request, and that fee goes up after launch
It doesn't; in an agile project a change costs about the same at every stage of the work
practice.answer: Everything built on the old requirement, from design to training, must be reworked and retested
practice.why: Every artifact built on a decision has to change when the decision does, so late changes multiply the rework, the retesting and the risk, and after launch they also touch live data and real users. No model forbids change; models differ in how they control it. Vendor pricing varies and isn't the reason the cost rises. Agile lowers the cost of change with small increments and automated tests, but a late change still costs more than catching it early.

pitfalls: Visuals that don't match the proposal. A 2025 student was returned three times because the diagrams didn't match the CRM described. Use the same feature names, fields and steps as your requirements, and explain each visual.

Ignoring the provided documents. The requirements document and design template define the scenario. The reported advice is to mirror their wording, label each requirement in its subsection and pull hosting details from the requirements document.
Coming up short on counts. Count what your rubric asks for in each list, such as prerequisites, goals and objectives, and meet it; a commenter's paper came back over a missing prerequisite.
Blurring goals and objectives. Goals are broad outcomes, while objectives are measurable and time-bound. An objective without a number or a date will read as a goal.

Non-functional requirements with no numbers. "Secure", "fast" and "easy to use" can't be tested. Give each one a target, such as a response time, an uptime percentage or a WCAG level, plus the conditions it applies under.
Generic methodology arguments. Saying agile is flexible isn't a justification. Compare the candidates on the same criteria and tie your choice to the scenario's facts.
Test cases nobody else could run. Missing preconditions, steps, data or expected results make a test case unreplicable, and students advise leaving stress tests out.
Visuals of the wrong kind. Pick a diagram that fits what it shows, such as a screen mockup for a layout and a flowchart for a process, and explain each one.
Writing more than the rubric asks. Recent replies say to keep it simple and cover exactly what the rubric asks. Extra material gives an evaluator more to question without earning credit.

community.summary: Students' advice is consistent: follow the rubric letter by letter, mirror the requirements document and label every requirement. Experiences vary widely. An Apr 2024 first-try passer wrote 14 pages in about two days, and 2025 commenters say it can take only a few hours once the structure is clear, while a 2025 student was returned three times over visuals that didn't match the CRM even after instructors approved the content. The advice in that thread: keep it simple, cover exactly what the rubric asks, and if feedback contradicts the written requirements or instructor guidance, appeal with the emails.
